web_title: 1. Origin, Corporate Evolution & Past Business Cycles
book_title: From Ahmedabad Code Shop to Physical AI
question: How did an Ahmedabad software consultancy evolve into a capital-intensive robotics and programmatic media platform—and what business cycles has it weathered?

epigraph.quote: Hardware is hard not because the physics is mysterious, but because the balance sheet has to finance every mistake before the customer pays.
epigraph.author: Industrial Automation Adage

web_blocks.html: Kody Technolab Limited began in May 2017 in Ahmedabad, Gujarat. Manav Subhashchandra Patel, a mechanical engineer by training, founded the firm after stepping away from family businesses [3]. He partnered with Chief Executive Officer Sanjay Kidecha and promoter group members Manali Krunal Patel and Pooja Sunny Patel [3]. For its first five years, Kody ran as a boutique IT services shop. The team built custom web apps, mobile tools, and machine-learning software for Indian and overseas clients [3].

web_blocks.title: The Pivot to Physical AI and the 2023 NSE Emerge Listing

web_blocks.html: Management did not stay in pure IT services. They used early software cash flows to open R&D labs, including a branch in Gujarat's GIFT City (Gandhinagar) [3]. Engineers paired computer vision, LiDAR navigation, and AI software with physical robot frames [3, 5]. That shift created the Kody Robots product line. In September 2023, Kody Technolab listed on the NSE Emerge SME exchange [3]. The IPO opened on September 15, 2023, at ₹160 per share to fund robotics R&D and plant setup [3].

web_blocks.takeaway: Kody Technolab shifted from an asset-light IT firm (₹15 Cr fixed assets + CWIP in Mar 2025) to a capital-heavy robotics, EMS, and pDOOH operator (₹86 Cr fixed assets in Sep 2026) in 18 months.

web_blocks.title: Three Distinct Business Cycles Inside Nine Years

web_blocks.html: Even as a young firm, Kody has already crossed three distinct operating cycles. Cycle 1 (2017–2022) was an asset-light software phase. Margins tracked engineer billing rates, and working capital stayed low. Cycle 2 (2023–FY25) was the proof-of-concept robotics cycle. Demos at the Vibrant Gujarat Summit and Gujarat Police Expo raised domestic visibility [5]. FY25 consolidated sales hit ₹72 Cr with a 35% operating margin, though debtor days stretched to 177 days [1].

Cycle 3 (FY26–H1 FY27) is the industrial scaling cycle. Kody raised fresh equity via preferential shares and convertible warrants (25% upfront, 75% on conversion) and issued a 1:1 bonus [4]. Management formed Kody Media Limited for programmatic Digital Out-of-Home (pDOOH) ads [2]. They also launched Kody Middle East Holding LLC and the Falcon Tech Robotics LLC joint venture in the UAE [6]. At home, Kody invested in World EMS Private Limited for bulk robot assembly [7].

Cycle 3 reshaped the balance sheet fast. Between March 2025 and September 2026, total assets nearly tripled from ₹112 Cr to ₹298 Cr [1]. Sales grew +12% in FY26 to ₹80 Cr. Then H1 FY27 sales surged +97% YoY to ₹62 Cr, lifting TTM sales to ₹111 Cr [1]. Yet operating margins fell 1,600 basis points from 35% in FY25 to 19% in H1 FY27 [1]. Over the same span, working capital days jumped from 62 days to 197 days [1].

web_blocks.title: Forensic Checkpoint: When Growth Changes the Accounting Engine
paragraphs: When an IT firm shifts into hardware and Robot-as-a-Service (RaaS), sales growth is easy to cheer. It is also risky to take at face value. In H1 FY27, Kody's revenue nearly doubled YoY to ₹62 Cr. Yet consolidated net profit was ₹5 Cr, barely above ₹4 Cr a year earlier [1]. Depreciation jumped fourfold from ₹1 Cr to ₹4 Cr, operating costs rose from ₹24 Cr to ₹51 Cr, and the tax rate hit 47% [1].

web_blocks.html: From its September 2023 IPO through September 2025, promoter holding stayed flat at 73.01% [1]. Over the next four quarters, promoter stake dropped to 72.73% (Mar 2026), 69.49% (Sep 2026), and 68.82% (Oct 2026) [1]. That 419-basis-point decline reflects non-promoter warrant dilution and open-market sales by MD Manav Subhashchandra Patel [4]. Meanwhile, the board cleared up to ₹100 Cr in unsecured promoter credit lines in H1 FY27 [7]. External debt also climbed from ₹8 Cr (Mar 2026) to ₹27 Cr (Sep 2026), showing the cash hunger of Cycle 3 [1].

This rapid shift from software to hardware sets up the central question of our audit. Can Kody turn its ₹86 Cr fixed-asset base into steady cash flow? Or will working capital and depreciation keep absorbing every rupee of new equity and debt [1]? The answer depends on how fast deployed robots pay back their build costs and whether domestic and Gulf receivables collect on time [1, 6].

book_paragraphs: If you want to understand Kody Technolab without getting hypnotized by the buzzwords of 'Physical AI' and 'humanoid robotics,' you and I have to start at the beginning—in an Ahmedabad software office in May 2017. Manav Subhashchandra Patel, trained as a mechanical engineer, did not start Kody as a factory. He started it alongside CEO Sanjay Kidecha as a custom software and mobile-app consultancy. For years, the business ran on the cleanest economic engine in corporate India: sell engineering hours, collect client retainers, keep fixed assets minimal, and reinvest the surplus.

Most boutique IT firms stay in that lane forever because the cash is comfortable. Kody did not. Using its software cash flows and an R&D outpost in Gujarat's GIFT City, management began marrying computer vision, LiDAR navigation, and AI software stacks to physical robotic frames. By September 2023, that ambition took the company public on the NSE Emerge SME exchange at ₹160 per share. On paper, it looked like a classic Indian deep-tech origin story: engineers graduating from outsourced code to proprietary machines.

What you and I must examine closely, however, is how violently the underlying business cycle has shifted since that listing. Over the past nine years, Kody has not lived through one steady compounding arc; it has lived through three completely different industrial regimes. In the first regime, from 2017 to 2022, capital intensity was near zero. In the second regime, spanning the IPO through FY25, Kody showcased autonomous robots like Athena and Dasher at high-profile venues—the Vibrant Gujarat Summit, the Gujarat Police Expo, and GIFT City festivals—while software still anchored a lush 35% consolidated operating margin on ₹72 crore of revenue.

Then came the third regime in FY26 and H1 FY27, and this is where every serious investor needs to put on a forensic lens. Management decided not merely to build robots on order, but to own the entire value chain: electronics assembly through a tie-up with World EMS Private Limited, international distribution through Falcon Tech Robotics LLC in the UAE, and a robotics-powered programmatic Digital Out-of-Home advertising network through Kody Media Limited.

Look at what that strategic leap did to the balance sheet in just eighteen months. Between March 2025 and September 2026, total assets expanded from ₹112 crore to ₹298 crore. Fixed assets plus capital work-in-progress jumped nearly sixfold from ₹15 crore to ₹86 crore. To pay for that buildout, Kody tapped non-promoter investors through preferential shares and convertible warrants—bringing in ₹113 crore of financing cash flow in FY26—and then increased borrowings from ₹8 crore to ₹27 crore by September 2026.

Meanwhile, the income statement sent a split signal. Top-line growth exploded in the first half of FY27, jumping 97% year-on-year to ₹62 crore. Yet operating margins slid from 35% in FY25 to 30% in FY26 and down to 19% in September 2026. At the same time, promoter ownership edged down from 73.01% to 68.82% by October 2026 through a mix of warrant dilution and open-market sales by the Managing Director. When a business trades 35% software margins and near-zero fixed assets for 19% hardware-and-media margins and 197 working capital days, you and I cannot evaluate it on yesterday's software economics. We have to audit whether the new industrial machine actually earns its keep.

Let us also examine why the corporate structure changed so rapidly between FY25 and H1 FY27. In its early years, Kody's software engineers worked out of Ahmedabad offices and delivered digital products to clients who paid on milestone invoices. There was no need for a Dubai holding company, no need for an electronics manufacturing services partner, and no need for ₹86 crore of fixed assets. Once management decided to build a fleet of autonomous robots—Odigo for retail malls, Athena for perimeter security, Dasher for hospitality, and Medigo for health screening—the old corporate wrapper could not hold the new operational weight.

Each new entity solved a specific commercial bottleneck while introducing a new layer of financial complexity. World EMS Private Limited was brought into the fold to secure bulk electronics assembly and keep hardware bill-of-materials costs under control. Falcon Tech Robotics LLC was structured in the UAE with the Platinum Group to win regional distribution and manufacturing mandates across the Gulf Cooperation Council. Kody Middle East Holding LLC and Kody Media Limited were created to monetize robots not merely as one-off equipment sales, but as moving programmatic Digital Out-of-Home advertising screens.

From an engineering standpoint, that vertical integration is coherent. From an accounting and capital-allocation standpoint, however, it compresses three normally separate businesses—an IT consultancy, a robotics OEM, and an outdoor media network—into a single consolidated balance sheet. That is why you and I must resist the temptation to treat Kody's nine-year history as one continuous curve. The company we are underwriting today is less than two years old in its current industrial form.

Pause for a moment and consider what that means for historical comparisons. Any financial ratio from FY24 or FY25 reflects a software-heavy business with minimal depreciation and no large robot fleet on its books. By contrast, H1 FY27 reflects a hardware-and-media operator carrying ₹86 crore of fixed assets, ₹27 crore of debt, and a ₹100 crore promoter credit backstop. Our job in the chapters ahead is to dissect that new entity piece by piece.

Every investor who studies Indian SME transitions eventually encounters this exact fork in the road. A founder spots a larger, more exciting market—here, autonomous robots and programmatic media—and bets the balance sheet to reach it. Sometimes that leap builds an enduring industrial leader. Other times, the shift traps capital in slow-paying receivables and depreciating hardware while the original software cash cow gets overshadowed. Keeping both possibilities open is how you stay objective.

Remember that good analysis never confuses ambition with execution. Kody's founders showed real drive in taking an Ahmedabad software shop onto NSE Emerge and into UAE retail malls. Our task now is to measure whether the underlying business model is compounding capital or simply consuming it.

book_callouts.title: The Three-Regime Rule
book_callouts.text: Never extrapolate margins from Regime 2 (asset-light software + prototype demos) onto Regime 3 (owned manufacturing, RaaS fleets, and ad-network capex). The cost structure, depreciation curve, and working-capital hunger of the third regime are fundamentally different.
